questions.prompt: Which best describes a game engine?
choices: A reusable software layer providing general systems such as rendering, physics, audio, input, and asset loading
The set of rules and levels that make one specific game unique
A graphics card driver that draws triangles
A tool artists use only to paint textures
questions.answer: A reusable software layer providing general systems such as rendering, physics, audio, input, and asset loading
questions.explanation: An engine is the reusable layer beneath the game; the game itself supplies its own rules and content.

questions.prompt: Game-specific rules such as "when an enemy touches the player, subtract 10 health" belong in game code, not in the engine's collision system.
questions.explanation: Code that encodes one game's rules is game code; the engine should stay generic so it can be reused.

questions.prompt: Match each engine subsystem to its job.
pairs: Draws the world to the screen
Reads keyboard, mouse, and controller actions
questions.explanation: Each subsystem owns one category of work and exposes a defined interface to the rest of the engine.

questions.prompt: A character moves with `position += 5` once per frame, with no delta time. At 30 FPS, how many units does it move in one real second?
questions.explanation: 5 units per frame times 30 frames is 150 units per second, which is why the speed changes with frame rate.

questions.prompt: A fixed-timestep loop adds each real frame time (in milliseconds) to an accumulator, then runs one update for every full `step` it can subtract from the accumulator. Write `fixed_steps(frame_times, step)` that returns the total number of fixed updates run over all the frames. The accumulator carries leftover time into the next frame.
questions.explanation: Accumulate time, then subtract one step at a time while a full step remains, counting each update.

questions.prompt: Put the three phases of one game loop iteration in order.
questions.explanation: Render comes last so the screen shows the world after this frame's changes.

questions.prompt: Which statements about an Entity-Component-System (ECS) are true?
choices: An entity can be just an integer ID
A component is a plain bundle of data
A system runs logic over entities that have the components it needs
A component stores methods that entities inherit from it
Adding a Flying behavior requires creating a new subclass
answers: An entity can be just an integer ID
A component is a plain bundle of data
A system runs logic over entities that have the components it needs
questions.explanation: ECS replaces class hierarchies with IDs, data components, and systems; new behavior is a new component, not a subclass.

questions.prompt: In an ECS, what is the name for a plain bundle of data, such as Position or Health, attached to an entity?
questions.explanation: Components hold data only; systems supply the behavior.

questions.prompt: A movement system moves every entity by its velocity. Write `move_all(positions, velocities, dt)` where `positions` and `velocities` are lists of `[x, y]` pairs in the same order. Return a new list of positions where each is `position + velocity * dt`.
questions.reference:
def move_all(positions, velocities, dt):
    return [[p[0] + v[0] * dt, p[1] + v[1] * dt] for p, v in zip(positions, velocities)]
questions.explanation: For each pair, add velocity times dt to each coordinate, just like the lesson's MovementSystem.

questions.prompt: Put the render pipeline stages in order for a single triangle.
questions.explanation: Vertices are placed on screen first, rasterization finds covered pixels, fragments are colored, then the result is written to the framebuffer.

questions.prompt: What does frustum culling do?
choices: Discards objects entirely outside the camera's view before they are drawn
Lowers the triangle count of distant objects
Merges several draw calls into one
Compresses textures for the GPU
questions.answer: Discards objects entirely outside the camera's view before they are drawn
questions.explanation: Culling skips objects the camera cannot see, so no GPU time is spent on them.

questions.prompt: In a scene graph, each node's transform is stored relative to its parent, so rotating a parent also moves all of its children.
questions.explanation: A child's world position is computed by combining its local transform with its parent's, so changes to the parent carry down the tree.

questions.prompt: Write `aabb_overlap(a, b)` where each box is `[min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y]`. Return `True` if the boxes overlap and `False` otherwise. Boxes that only touch along an edge do not count as overlapping.
questions.reference:
def aabb_overlap(a, b):
    return a[0] < b[2] and b[0] < a[2] and a[1] < b[3] and b[1] < a[3]
questions.explanation: Two AABBs overlap only if their x-ranges overlap and their y-ranges overlap, which is four comparisons.

questions.prompt: A ball starts at rest. Each step uses `velocity += acceleration * dt` with acceleration -9.8 m/s² and dt = 0.1 s. What is the velocity in m/s after three steps? Give the answer to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Each step adds -9.8 times 0.1 = -0.98 m/s, so three steps give -2.94 m/s.

questions.prompt: Match each part of a physics step to what it does.
pairs: Cheap checks that discard pairs far apart
Exact shape test on pairs that survive
Pushes overlapping bodies apart and updates velocities
Updates velocity and position each timestep
questions.explanation: A physics engine runs all four parts every fixed step.

questions.prompt: Why does an engine convert source assets (such as .png or .blend files) into runtime assets during development?
choices: Runtime formats load fast, and the slow conversion is paid once instead of at every launch
Source formats cannot store textures or models
It lets players edit the assets in the game
It removes the need for a memory budget
questions.answer: Runtime formats load fast, and the slow conversion is paid once instead of at every launch
questions.explanation: Source formats are built for editing; baking them ahead of time into a fast runtime format keeps load times short.

questions.prompt: A game has a 100 MB asset budget and currently has a 20 MB texture and a 45 MB model loaded. It now needs to load a 60 MB level. At minimum, how many MB of loaded assets must be evicted first?
questions.explanation: 20 + 45 + 60 = 125 MB, which is 25 MB over the 100 MB budget.

questions.prompt: Level of detail (LOD) alone reduces memory use, because distant objects are simply not stored in memory.
questions.explanation: LOD only reduces rendering cost; the object data is still resident. Streaming is what saves memory.

questions.prompt: Explain why engines usually pair a fast compiled core with a scripting layer, and what each side is best at.
rubric: Says the core (rendering, physics, ECS) is in a fast compiled language
Says compiling takes time, which slows tweaking gameplay
Says the scripting layer lets designers change game logic quickly without recompiling
Says scripting is slower, so heavy per-frame work stays in the core
questions.model: The core is written in a compiled language like C++ for speed, but recompiling takes minutes, which is painful when a designer wants to tune a jump height. A scripting language like Lua holds game-specific logic and can be changed quickly. It is slower, so heavy work like physics and rendering stays in the core.
questions.explanation: The split trades raw performance in the core for iteration speed in the game logic.

questions.prompt: Put these parts of one frame in the order an engine runs them.
items: Scripts read input and set the player's velocity
Physics integrates movement and resolves collisions
questions.explanation: Each stage needs the freshest result of the one before it: intent, then physics, then final transforms, then drawing.

questions.prompt: Why is an explicit state machine better than separate flags like `isPaused` and `isGameOver`?
choices: It is always in exactly one state, so impossible combinations cannot occur
It makes the game run at a higher frame rate
It removes the need for scenes
It lets several states be active together
questions.answer: It is always in exactly one state, so impossible combinations cannot occur
questions.explanation: Separate booleans can accidentally both be true; a state machine permits only defined states and transitions.
